tldr: Rather than discretizing full trajectories over time, this paper introduces SCI, a novel method that optimizes only the contact points where robots reach minimum separation. It can plan collision-free motion for one million robots in just minutes.
hero_caption: Snapshots showing 1,000 robots transitioning from a planar grid into a double-helix formation, along with scaling of contact counts and computation times up to one million robots. Computation time scales nearly linearly even as fleet size surges.
overview:
Applications needing safe, smooth coordination for massive robot fleets—from drone light shows to automated guided vehicles—are expanding rapidly. However, generating collision-free trajectories becomes an intractable nonconvex optimization problem as the number of robots grows, due to combinatorial explosion and complex constraints. Existing approaches typically discretize time and optimize positions and velocities at all time steps simultaneously (such as Sequential Convex Programming, or SCP), but these demand prohibitive computation times even for hundreds or thousands of robots.

The authors observed that moments where robots actually get closest and must actively avoid each other (contact points) are quite rare, and optimal trajectory segments between contacts can be solved analytically. They formulate an algebraic system strictly around the times and states of these contacts—points where relative distance hits the safety limit—and bridge the intervals analytically via cubic Hermite polynomials.

Building on this insight, they developed Sequential Contact Insertion (SCI). The algorithm starts with unconstrained trajectories, inserts contact points wherever separation violations occur, and adjusts all contacts jointly. In experiments, SCI solved collision-free trajectory planning for one million ($10^6$) robots in roughly eight and a half minutes (525 seconds), and planned for 1,000 robots in a mere 0.12 seconds, showing breathtaking scalability and speed.
contributions: Established a contact-based optimization framework that models minimum separation constraints as point contacts and reconstructs inter-contact trajectories analytically via cubic polynomials.
Developed the Sequential Contact Insertion (SCI) algorithm, which sequentially inserts contacts at violation points and jointly adjusts contact times and states using coupled algebraic equations.
Leveraged contact graphs to decompose interacting fleets into independent connected components, enabling ultra-fast solves via the block tridiagonal structure of the Jacobian.
Demonstrated trajectory planning for mega-fleets of one million robots in minutes, delivering median speedups of several orders of magnitude over a standard SCP baseline.

sections.heading: Formulating the problem: barycenter and relative motion decomposition
sections.summary: Robot fleets are modeled using double-integrator dynamics to formulate an energy-minimization problem subject to collision-avoidance constraints. Decomposing motion into fleet barycenter and relative coordinates clarifies the theoretical behavior at contacts.
sections.details:
### II-A Fleet modeling
Consider $N$ robots operating in $d$-dimensional space (typically 2D or 3D) over a fixed time horizon $[0, T]$. Each robot is assigned initial and terminal positions and velocities. Robot dynamics follow a double-integrator model (acceleration as control input), a standard choice for high-level multi-robot planning. The objective is to minimize total energy, defined as the integral of squared accelerations across all robots. Constraints include pairwise collision avoidance—requiring the Euclidean distance between any two robots to remain at or above a minimum separation $R$—along with box limits on position, velocity, and acceleration.

### II-B The beauty of barycentric decomposition
To make this problem tractable, the system state is split into the fleet barycenter (average position) and coordinates relative to that barycenter. This decomposition is remarkably elegant. Pairwise collisions depend solely on relative coordinates. Without box constraints, the motion of the overall barycenter decouples completely, reducing to a simple cubic Hermite interpolant between boundary conditions.

### II-C Necessary conditions for optimal trajectories
Applying optimal control theory (such as Pontryagin's Minimum Principle) shows that away from active collision constraints (where distance equals $R$), trajectories are smooth cubic polynomials because no constraint forces act on them. At contact points, however, an instantaneous jump occurs in jerk (the derivative of acceleration), directed equally and oppositely along the line connecting the two robots. Consequently, one does not need fine-grained trajectory tracking: knowing when, in which direction, and with what force contacts occur is sufficient to reconstruct the full trajectory uniquely.

sections.heading: Connecting contacts: analytical trajectory reconstruction
sections.summary: Inter-robot contacts are represented as a finite set of points, yielding a system of matching equations based on contact and continuity conditions. Trajectories are reconstructed strictly from contact variables without temporal discretization.
sections.details:
### III-A Finite contact representation and contact graphs
The Lagrange multipliers enforcing separation constraints are approximated as a finite collection of point contacts. Each contact is characterized by its robot pair, timestamp, normal direction, and contact multiplier (magnitude). By defining a contact graph with robots as nodes and contacts as edges, the entire system cleanly decouples into independent connected components of interacting robots.

### III-B Matching equations
Within each contact component, physical consistency conditions are enforced at every contact: continuity of acceleration, matching jerk jumps with contact forces, and orthogonality of relative velocity to the contact normal. Assembling these yields a nonlinear system $F(c) = 0$. Crucially, each contact equation couples only with its immediate temporal neighbors on the trajectory, giving the Jacobian matrix a block tridiagonal (banded) structure. When applying Newton's method, the system can be solved in linear time ($O(m)$) with respect to the number of contacts $m$.

### Handling sustained contacts and box constraints
What happens during prolonged grazing encounters (sustained contact)? The authors approximate sustained interactions by clustering multiple discrete point contacts along the time axis, achieving ample accuracy in practice. When velocity or acceleration box constraints are present, an auxiliary momentum formulation with piecewise-linear updates extends the analytical machinery naturally.

sections.heading: Inside the Sequential Contact Insertion (SCI) algorithm
sections.summary: SCI begins with an unconstrained cubic trajectory, detects the most severe separation violations, and iteratively inserts contacts while resolving the matching equations.
sections.details:
Sequential Contact Insertion (SCI) operates as a greedy active-set strategy coupled with Newton's method. It iterates through the following stages until convergence:

- Grouping: Tracks robot interactions via the contact graph. When a new contact is added, only the affected components are merged, leaving unrelated robot groups untouched.
- Matching: Solves the coupled matching equations $F(c) = 0$ for each affected group using a damped Newton's method. Because Jacobians are derived analytically and possess banded structure, this step is blazingly fast. If a local solve yields negative multipliers (representing non-physical attractive forces), root deflation is applied to steer the solver toward valid roots.
- Detection: Sweeps continuous-time trajectories to locate robot pairs with minimum separation or constraint violations. Using the convex-hull property of Bernstein polynomials within a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH), distant pairs are pruned aggressively.
- Insertion: If a separation falls below $R$, a contact is inserted at the time of maximum penetration, initialized with zero contact force, and the system is resolved.

The algorithm also prunes inactive contacts whose multipliers drop to zero, keeping the active set compact and efficient.

sections.heading: Numerical results: from 1,000,000 robots to SCP benchmarks
sections.summary: Experiments ranging from a million-robot double-helix transition to head-to-head comparisons against SCP demonstrate multi-order-of-magnitude speedups and strict continuous-time safety.
sections.details:
All benchmarks ran on a standard consumer laptop (Apple M3 Pro, 36 GB RAM), benchmarked against a fixed-grid Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) baseline (200 grid points, using the OSQP solver).

### Experiment 1: One million robots formation transition
Robots were tasked with transitioning from a planar grid into a 3D double-helix structure. Robot counts scaled from 500 up to 1,000,000. Planning for 1,000 robots (118 contacts) took only 0.124 seconds. Remarkably, planning for 1,000,000 robots (151,071 contacts) finished in 525.4 seconds (around 8 minutes 45 seconds)—an unprecedented scale in multi-robot motion planning.

### Experiments 2 & 3: Speed and accuracy vs. SCP
On a benchmark with $N=20$ robots, SCI achieved a median runtime of 0.009 seconds compared to 106.6 seconds for SCP—a 12,289x speedup. Trajectory safety was even more striking: because SCP only enforces collision avoidance on discrete grid points, inter-sample interpenetrations caused a continuous-time success rate of $0\%$ (median interpenetration of $2.8\%$ of $R$). In contrast, SCI accounts for contacts analytically in continuous time, maintaining a $100\%$ success rate. When tighter tolerance requirements were tested, SCI solved instances with minimal time penalties, yielding speedups exceeding 80,000x.

### Experiments 4–7: Crowding, dimensionality, and box constraints
Under high-density spatial crowding and across dimensions scaling to 3D, 5D, and 10D, SCI runtimes remained in the sub-millisecond to millisecond range. Over 102 test cases with velocity and acceleration box limits, SCI maintained the same median runtime of 0.20 seconds as in the unconstrained case, proving robust under realistic physical constraints.

sections.heading: Conclusion: contact-based optimization redefines multi-agent planning
sections.summary: By focusing on continuous-time contacts, SCI plans trajectories for thousands of robots in fractions of a second and a million robots in minutes, pairing analytical rigor with extreme speed.
sections.details: The key breakthrough of this work lies in replacing brute-force spatio-temporal discretizations with an analytical insight from optimal control: optimal trajectories are smooth polynomials everywhere except at contact instants. Combining contact-graph decomposition with banded Newton solves reduces a multi-million-dimensional nonconvex problem to an efficient, deterministic sequence of linear-time steps. Future directions include extensions to cluttered obstacle-filled environments, dynamic settings, and online deployment on real-world drone swarms.

takeaways: Optimizing strictly over active constraint events (contacts) rather than discretizing the full trajectory is exceptionally powerful for mega-scale trajectory planning.
Stationarity conditions from optimal control yield a block tridiagonal Jacobian, allowing Newton updates to run in linear time with respect to contact count.
While grid-based SCP frequently suffers from inter-sample collision violations, the analytical formulation guarantees exact safety in continuous time.
Planning for 1,000 robots in 0.1 seconds and 1,000,000 robots in minutes fundamentally shifts assumptions around real-time swarm control and drone light show design.
limitations: Robot motion is modeled as double integrators (acceleration inputs), delegating higher-order nonlinear aerodynamics and attitude dynamics to lower-level onboard controllers.
Sustained, continuous contacts must be approximated by clustering multiple discrete point contacts, which can increase the contact count and computational burden.
Evaluations focused primarily on open spaces and formation swaps with high spatial symmetry, rather than densely cluttered static environments such as complex mazes.
